title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

errors: Top of page: 'Dum autem sol est in apogeo, variatio ... ne ad dimidium quidem minutum secundum ascendit' should logically read 'luna est in apogeo'. The half-second bound refers to the ±0.4" coefficient of cos V when the Moon is at apogee. With the Sun at apogee and the Moon at perigee the solar term is 3.2". This looks like a slip in the manuscript or the printed text (the image does read 'sol').

Small internal inconsistency: setting η=0 in the §15 series gives about −258.1 cos v (−216.4 − 0.6 − 41.1; with the logarithmic values 216.36 + 0.64 + 41.11 = 258.1). The conjunction formula on the previous page has −258.3 (log 2.41212). Likewise cos 2v gives 11.75 against 11.7 (consistent), and the opposition constant gives 2023.0 against 33'43.1" = 2023.1. These are discrepancies of about 0.1–0.2".

Setting η=0 in the §15 series also produces a cos(v+V) term, −0.7 + 0.4 = −0.3", which is absent from the previous page's conjunction formula. It is negligible, but inconsistent with the tenth-of-a-second precision he recommends.

The claim that the minimum hourly motion falls exactly at quadrature is only approximately true for his own series. At v=0 the variation and evection terms nearly cancel, leaving f(η) = 1.2 cos 2η − 1.1 cos η, which is smallest near cos η ≈ 0.23 (η ≈ 77°). That point lies about 0.13" below the quadrature value. This is immaterial at his stated precision.

Rounding: at the Moon's apogee with the Sun at perigee the formula gives 1773.2 − 1.7 = 1771.5", reported as 1771" (29'31"). At the Moon's perigee with the Sun at apogee it gives 2126.5", reported as 2126". These are acceptable truncations.

ideas.what: Hourly lunar motion obtained as a trigonometric series, by differentiating the longitude series, in the anomaly v, the solar anomaly V and the elongation η, with coefficients given as logarithms
ideas.modern_name: Time-derivative of the lunar longitude series (lunar velocity / horary motion series)
ideas.usually_credited_to: General practice of 18th-century lunar theory (Euler, Mayer, Clairaut); horary-motion tables appear in later ephemerides
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar theories (E187 Theoria motus lunae 1753; E418 Theoria motuum lunae 1772) treat the longitude series. A separate hourly-motion series is not known to me in them.

ideas.what: Proposal for a dedicated hourly-motion table in twelve parts, given to tenths of an arcsecond so the accumulated error stays below 1", for eclipses and occultations
ideas.modern_name: Auxiliary horary-motion table / error budgeting of tabulated equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard in later almanac practice (e.g. Nautical Almanac horary motions)

ideas.what: Evaluation of the extremes of the Moon's hourly motion: minimum at quadrature with Moon at apogee and Sun at perigee; maximum at opposition with both at perigee
ideas.modern_name: Extrema of lunar angular velocity under the equation of centre, variation and evection

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries out routine numerical consequences of a lunar hourly-motion series and gives a practical tabulation proposal. The arithmetic checks out apart from minor 0.1–0.2" inconsistencies and one apparent slip ('sol' for 'luna'). Nothing here would be new to a historian of 18th-century lunar theory.
transcription_corrections: §15 opening: 'ita se habebit, ut [?]' – the image shows 'habebit, ut' with the right margin damaged. The '[?]' is just the reading 'ut' cut off at the margin.
The last term of the §15 series is '+ 0,4 cos(2η − v − V)'. This is cut off in the image but confirmed by the quadrature reduction, which gives −1.1 cos(v+V) = −0.7 − 0.4.
The header of the §16 column reads '⊙ in Perig.' (partly obscured); the values in that column are 1771" (29'31") and 2119" (35'19").
The logarithm under 0.5 cos V is 9.676 (i.e. log 0.474 with characteristic 9 for negative). The transcription is correct; the logs under the cos(v±V) terms are 9.858 and 9.846.
